translation.recipeClassicDesc: The essential sourdough bread — crispy crust, open crumb, incredible flavor
translation.recipeClassicStep1: Mix starter with water until dissolved
translation.recipeClassicStep2: Add flour, mix until no dry spots remain. Rest 30 min (autolyse)
translation.recipeClassicStep3: Add salt, knead gently for 5 minutes
translation.recipeClassicStep4: Stretch & fold every 30 min for 2 hours (4 sets)
translation.recipeClassicStep6: Shape into a ball, place in banneton, refrigerate 1-2 hours
translation.recipeClassicStep7: Bake in dutch oven: 25 min with lid at 230°C, then 20 min without lid
translation.recipeClassicTip: The dough should feel airy and jiggly after bulk fermentation. If it's dense, let it ferment longer.
translation.recipeWholeWheatDesc: Hearty and nutritious with a deeper, nuttier flavor
translation.recipeWholeWheatStep1: Mix starter with water, add flours. Rest 45 min (autolyse)
translation.recipeWholeWheatStep2: Add salt, stretch & fold every 30 min for 2.5 hours
translation.recipeWholeWheatStep4: Shape, proof in banneton in fridge for 1-2 hours
translation.recipeWholeWheatStep5: Bake at 230°C: 25 min covered, 20 min uncovered
translation.recipeWholeWheatTip: Whole wheat absorbs more water — don't be afraid of sticky dough. It will come together during folding.
translation.recipeRyeDesc: Dense, aromatic, and full of complex flavors — European style
translation.recipeRyeStep1: Mix everything together — no kneading needed for rye
translation.recipeRyeStep2: Pour into greased loaf pan, smooth top with wet hands
translation.recipeRyeStep3: Proof 3-5 hours at room temperature until risen by 50%
translation.recipeRyeStep4: Bake at 220°C for 50-60 min. Cool completely before slicing (2-3 hours!)
translation.recipeRyeTip: Rye bread MUST cool completely — cutting it warm makes it gummy. Patience pays off!
translation.recipeFocacciaDesc: Fluffy, olive-oil-rich Italian flatbread — perfect for beginners
translation.recipeFocacciaIng5: 4 tbsp olive oil + toppings (rosemary, olives, cherry tomatoes)
translation.recipeFocacciaStep1: Mix starter, water, flour. Rest 30 min, add salt and 2 tbsp olive oil
translation.recipeFocacciaStep2: Stretch & fold 3 times over 1.5 hours, then bulk ferment 8-10h
translation.recipeFocacciaStep3: Pour into oiled pan, dimple with fingers, drizzle olive oil, add toppings
translation.recipeFocacciaStep4: Proof 1 hour, then bake at 220°C for 20-25 minutes until golden
translation.recipeFocacciaTip: Be generous with olive oil — it's what makes focaccia special. The bottom should be slightly crispy.
translation.recipeCiabattaDesc: Rustic Italian bread with huge holes and crispy crust
translation.recipeCiabattaStep1: Mix all ingredients. The dough will be very wet — that's correct!
translation.recipeCiabattaStep2: Stretch & fold every 30 min for 3 hours (6 sets). Dough should be billowy
translation.recipeCiabattaStep3: Bulk ferment overnight. Pour onto floured surface, cut into rectangles
translation.recipeCiabattaStep4: Gently transfer to baking sheet — don't deflate the bubbles!
translation.recipeCiabattaStep5: Bake at 230°C with steam for 25-30 minutes
translation.recipeCiabattaTip: The secret to big holes is high hydration and gentle handling. Never punch down the dough.
translation.recipeBaguetteDesc: The ultimate baker’s test: crisp crust, airy crumb, and beautiful slashes. Practice makes the difference.
translation.recipeBaguetteStep1: Mix starter with water. Add flour and combine roughly.
translation.recipeBaguetteStep7: Pre-shape into rectangles, rest 20 minutes covered.
translation.recipeBaguetteStep8: Shape baguettes, roll tight, seal the seam.
translation.recipeBaguetteStep9: Proof on a floured couche with folds for support.
translation.recipeBaguetteStep11: Preheat oven to 250°C with stone or steel.
translation.recipeBaguetteStep13: Bake with steam 10 minutes, then 12-15 minutes without steam.
translation.recipeBaguetteTip: Scoring: hold the blade at 45° and move with confidence. Practice makes perfect baguettes!
translation.recipePancakesDesc: Fluffy, tangy pancakes — the best way to use discard
translation.recipePancakesStep1: Mix discard with egg, sugar, and melted butter
translation.recipePancakesStep2: Add baking soda right before cooking — it will bubble up!
translation.recipePancakesStep3: Cook on medium heat, flip when bubbles form on surface. About 2 min per side
translation.recipePancakesTip: Let the batter rest 10 min before cooking for extra fluffy pancakes.
translation.recipeCrackersStep1: Mix discard with olive oil and salt
translation.recipeCrackersStep2: Roll paper-thin on parchment, sprinkle with toppings
translation.recipeCrackersStep3: Bake at 180°C for 15-20 min until golden and crispy. Break into pieces
translation.recipeCrackersTip: The thinner you roll them, the crispier they get. Paper-thin is the goal!
translation.recipePizzaDesc: Best pizza dough you'll ever make — slow fermented for maximum flavor
translation.recipePizzaStep1: Mix all ingredients, knead 10 minutes until smooth
translation.recipePizzaStep2: Bulk ferment 6-8 hours (or overnight in fridge for more flavor)
translation.recipePizzaStep3: Divide into 2 balls, stretch into rounds on floured surface
translation.recipePizzaStep4: Top and bake at maximum oven temp (250°C+) for 8-12 minutes
translation.recipePizzaTip: Preheat your oven for at least 30 minutes with a baking stone/steel for the crispiest crust.
translation.recipeBananaBreadDesc: Moist, tender, and subtly tangy — discard makes it better
translation.recipeBananaBreadIng5: 1 tsp baking soda, pinch of salt
translation.recipeBananaBreadStep1: Mash bananas, mix with discard, egg, butter, and sugar
translation.recipeBananaBreadStep2: Fold in flour, baking soda, and salt — don't overmix!
translation.recipeBananaBreadStep3: Pour into greased loaf pan, bake at 175°C for 55-65 min
translation.recipeBananaBreadTip: The riper the bananas, the sweeter and moister the bread. Brown spotted bananas are perfect!
translation.recipeWafflesDesc: Crispy outside, fluffy inside — weekend breakfast perfection
translation.recipeWafflesStep1: Mix discard with eggs, melted butter, sugar, and vanilla
translation.recipeWafflesStep2: Add baking soda, stir gently (it will puff up!)
translation.recipeWafflesStep3: Cook in preheated waffle iron until golden and crispy
translation.recipeWafflesTip: For extra crispy waffles, let the batter rest overnight in the fridge.
translation.recipeBriocheDesc: Rich, buttery French bread — worth every minute of waiting
translation.recipeBriocheStep1: Mix starter, flour, eggs, sugar. Knead 10 min until smooth
translation.recipeBriocheStep2: Add butter piece by piece, knead until silky (10-15 min more)
translation.recipeBriocheStep4: Shape, proof 2-3 hours at room temp, egg wash, bake at 180°C for 25-30 min
translation.recipeBriocheTip: Cold butter won't incorporate well. Let it soften at room temperature for 1 hour before using.
translation.recipeBagelsDesc: Chewy, dense, and with that perfect crust — New York style
translation.recipeBagelsStep1: Mix all ingredients, knead 12-15 min until very smooth and elastic
translation.recipeBagelsStep2: Bulk ferment 4-6 hours, then divide into 8 pieces
translation.recipeBagelsStep3: Shape into rings, cold proof overnight in fridge
translation.recipeBagelsStep4: Boil each bagel 1 min per side in water with honey/malt
translation.recipeBagelsStep5: Add toppings (sesame, poppy, everything), bake at 220°C for 18-22 min
translation.recipeBagelsTip: The boiling step is what makes a bagel a bagel — never skip it! It creates that iconic chewy crust.
translation.recipeCinnamonDesc: Soft, gooey, and irresistible — slow fermented for better flavor
translation.recipeCinnamonIng3: Filling: 100g brown sugar, 2 tbsp cinnamon, 40g soft butter
translation.recipeCinnamonIng4: Glaze: 100g cream cheese, 60g powdered sugar, 1 tbsp milk
translation.recipeCinnamonStep1: Mix dough ingredients, knead until smooth. Bulk ferment 4-6 hours
translation.recipeCinnamonStep2: Roll into rectangle, spread butter, sugar-cinnamon filling
translation.recipeCinnamonStep3: Roll tightly, cut into 12 pieces, place in greased pan
translation.recipeCinnamonStep4: Proof overnight in fridge. Bake at 180°C for 25-30 min, top with cream cheese glaze
translation.recipeCinnamonTip: For the gooiest rolls, slightly underbake them. They'll firm up as they cool but stay soft inside.
translation.recipeMuffinsDesc: Perfect nooks and crannies — made on the stovetop
translation.recipeMuffinsStep1: Mix all ingredients (except cornmeal), knead 8 min. Bulk ferment 8-10 hours
translation.recipeMuffinsStep2: Roll out 2cm thick, cut rounds, dust with cornmeal on both sides
translation.recipeMuffinsStep3: Cook on low heat in dry skillet, 7-8 min per side until golden
translation.recipeMuffinsTip: Low heat is crucial — high heat will burn the outside before the inside is cooked. Be patient!
translation.recipePretzelsDesc: Soft, chewy pretzels with that classic deep brown crust
translation.recipePretzelsStep1: Mix and knead until smooth (10 min). Bulk ferment 4-6 hours
translation.recipePretzelsStep2: Divide into 8 pieces, roll into long ropes, shape into pretzels
translation.recipePretzelsStep3: Dip briefly in baking soda bath (1L water + 60g baking soda, boiled), sprinkle coarse salt
translation.recipePretzelsStep4: Bake at 220°C for 12-15 minutes until deep golden brown
translation.recipePretzelsTip: The baking soda bath is what gives pretzels their unique color and flavor. Don't skip it!
translation.dayGuideContent1:
Mix 50g rye flour + 50g warm water (28-30°C) in a clean jar.
Stir well until smooth — no dry lumps.
Mark the level with a rubber band and cover loosely.
Place in a warm spot (24-26°C). Now we wait!
translation.dayGuideContent2:
Don't touch it today — just observe.
You might see a few tiny bubbles or nothing at all.
Both are completely normal at this stage.
The bacteria are quietly colonizing the flour.
translation.dayGuideContent3:
Discard half (keep ~50g), then add:
50g white flour + 50g warm water.
Stir well, mark the new level, cover loosely.
You may notice a sour or yeasty smell — that's great!
translation.dayGuideContent4:
Feed again: discard half, add 50g flour + 50g water.
You might see a big rise followed by a collapse.
Don't worry — bad bacteria are being replaced by good ones.
The smell may be strong or strange. It will improve!
translation.dayGuideContent5:
Feed again: discard half, add 50g flour + 50g water.
Look for consistent small bubbles throughout.
The smell should be mellowing — slightly sour, like yogurt.
Your starter is finding its rhythm!
translation.dayGuideContent6:
Feed again: discard half, add 50g flour + 50g water.
The rise should be more predictable now.
Check every 2-3 hours to learn your starter's pace.
Tomorrow might be the big day!
translation.dayGuideContent7:
Feed and watch closely.
If it doubles in 4-6 hours — congratulations, it's ready!
If not quite there, don't worry — many starters need 10-14 days. Continue daily feeds.
Look for: volume doubling, lots of bubbles, a pleasant tangy smell.
translation.dayGuideContent8:
Your starter is maturing! Feed once daily at the same time.
Consistency is key — same time, same amounts.
Switch to 100% white flour if you haven't already.
Start observing peak timing more carefully.
translation.dayGuideContent9:
Temperature is your main control variable.
Warmer (26-28°C) = faster rise, more sour.
Cooler (20-22°C) = slower rise, milder flavor.
Find the sweet spot for your kitchen and schedule.
translation.dayGuideContent10:
Peak (PMC) is when your starter is at maximum rise.
It's domed on top, full of bubbles, jiggly.
This is the ideal moment for baking.
Mark the rubber band and note the hours to peak.
translation.dayGuideContent11:
Try feeding with a mix: 90% white + 10% whole wheat.
Different flours bring different nutrients and flavors.
Rye gives a tangy, robust character.
Whole wheat adds nuttiness. Find what you love!
translation.dayGuideContent12:
Your starter should now double reliably in 4-6 hours.
If it's sluggish, try warmer water or a warmer spot.
A strong starter means better bread.
Look for a domed top, honeycomb texture, and pleasant tangy aroma.
translation.dayGuideContent13:
Tomorrow you can bake your first bread!
Build a levain tonight: 25g starter + 50g flour + 50g water.
Let it ferment overnight (8-10 hours).
It should be bubbly and domed by morning.
translation.dayGuideContent14:
Your starter has completed its journey from flour and water to a living culture!
You now have a reliable sourdough starter.
From here: feed 2-3x/week, or store in the fridge between bakes.
Check the Learn section for your first bread recipe!
translation.dayTask1: Mix 50g rye flour with 50g warm water. Stir until smooth, cover loosely.
translation.dayTask1Content: Today you bring your starter to life! Use rye flour for the best start.
translation.dayTask2: Just observe today. Don't touch it! Look for any tiny bubbles forming.
translation.dayTask2Content: Patience is key. The bacteria need time to get established.
translation.dayTask3: Discard half, then add 50g white flour + 50g warm water. Mix well!
translation.dayTask3Content: From now on, we switch to white flour for consistent results.
translation.dayTask4: Discard half, add 50g flour + 50g water. Watch for rise and fall patterns.
translation.dayTask4Content: The starter might rise big then collapse — that's the bacterial transition!
translation.dayTask5: Same routine: discard half, feed 50g flour + 50g water. Notice the bubbles!
translation.dayTask5Content: You should see more consistent bubbling now. The good bacteria are winning!
translation.dayTask6: Feed as usual. Start checking every 2 hours to learn your starter's peak time.
translation.dayTask6Content: Understanding when your starter peaks is crucial for future baking.
translation.dayTask7: Feed and watch closely. Does it double in size? Is the texture bubbly and airy?
translation.dayTask7Content: If it doubles in 4-6 hours with lots of bubbles and a tangy aroma, you're ready to bake!
translation.lessonShort1: Why flour type matters and how water affects your starter
translation.lessonContent1:
Everything starts with flour and water. Flour provides the food (starch and sugars) that wild yeast and bacteria need. Different flours have different nutrients: - Rye flour: Rich in nutrients, great for starting a new culture
- White flour: Consistent and predictable, ideal for daily feeding
- Whole wheat: Extra minerals and fiber, good for occasional variety Water quality matters too:
- Use filtered or bottled water if your tap water is heavily chlorinated
- Warm water (25-30°C) speeds up fermentation
- Cold water slows it down — useful for timing control The standard ratio is 1:1:1 — equal parts starter, flour, and water by weight. Always use a scale, not measuring cups!
translation.lessonShort2: How temperature affects fermentation speed and flavor
translation.lessonContent2:
Temperature is the single most important variable you can control. Warm (26-28°C):
- Faster fermentation (peak in 4-5 hours)
- More lactic acid = milder, creamy flavor
- Better for when you want to bake quickly Cool (20-22°C):
- Slower fermentation (peak in 8-12 hours)
- More acetic acid = tangier, more complex flavor
- Better for overnight timing Cold (fridge, 4°C):
- Nearly stops fermentation
- Use for storage between bakes
- Take out 24 hours before you want to bake Tips:
- Keep your starter in the warmest spot of your kitchen
- A turned-off oven with just the light on is often 26-28°C
- Use a thermometer to learn your kitchen's microclimates
translation.lessonShort3: What 100% hydration means and how to adjust it
translation.lessonContent3:
Hydration is the ratio of water to flour in your starter. 100% hydration (1:1 water to flour):
- Most common and easiest to maintain
- Consistency like thick pancake batter
- Rises high and is easy to observe 80% hydration:
- Slightly thicker, like cookie dough
- Rises slower but more predictably
- Some bakers prefer it for bread with less sour flavor 60% hydration (stiff starter):
- Very thick, like firm dough
- Develops more acetic acid (vinegar tang)
- Used in some traditional European breads For beginners, stick with 100% hydration. It's the most forgiving and easiest to read. You can experiment with different hydrations once you're comfortable with the basics.
translation.lessonShort4: How to identify when your starter is at its strongest
translation.lessonContent4:
The peak — or Point of Maximum Rise (PMC) — is when your starter is at its strongest and most active. This is the moment to use it for baking. Signs of peak:
- Doubled (or more) in volume from the marked line
- Domed on top, not flat or sunken
- Full of visible bubbles throughout
- Jiggly when you tap the jar
- Light and airy when scooped
- Pleasant, mildly sour smell These signs together are more reliable than any single test. Timing your peak:
- After feeding, check every 1-2 hours
- Note how many hours it takes to peak
- Use this knowledge to plan your baking schedule After peak, the starter begins to collapse and weaken. If you miss the window, just feed again and wait.
translation.lessonShort5: What's actually happening inside your starter
translation.lessonContent5:
Your starter is a living ecosystem of wild yeast and lactic acid bacteria (LAB). The cast of characters:
- Wild yeast (mainly Saccharomyces): Produces CO2 gas (the bubbles!) and alcohol
- Lactobacillus: Produces lactic acid (creamy sourness)
- Acetobacter: Produces acetic acid (vinegar tang) The fermentation cycle:
1. You feed flour and water
2. Bacteria and yeast consume the sugars
3. They produce gas, acids, and flavor compounds
4. The starter rises as gas gets trapped
5. Eventually food runs out and it collapses
6. Time to feed again! Why discard before feeding:
- Keeps the population balanced
- Prevents over-acidification
- Ensures enough food for the remaining organisms The entire ecosystem self-regulates. Your job is just to keep feeding it consistently!
translation.lessonShort6: Step-by-step guide to baking your first sourdough loaf
translation.lessonContent6:
You've been waiting for this! Here's your first bread, simplified. Ingredients:
- 100g active starter (at peak)
- 400g white flour
- 280g water (25-30°C)
- 8g salt The process:
1. Mix starter + water until dissolved
2. Add flour, mix until no dry spots. Rest 30 min (autolyse)
3. Add salt, knead gently 5 minutes
4. Stretch & fold every 30 min for 2 hours (4 sets)
5. Let it ferment overnight (8-12 hours at room temp)
6. Shape into a ball, place in banneton
7. Refrigerate 1-2 hours
8. Bake in dutch oven: 25 min with lid at 230°C, 20 min without Don't worry if your first loaf isn't perfect. The flavor will still be incredible! Each loaf teaches you something new.
translation.lessonShort7: How to keep your starter healthy long-term
translation.lessonContent7:
Once your starter is established, maintenance is easy. Active schedule (baking 2-3x per week):
- Feed once daily at room temperature
- Use for baking when at peak Low-maintenance schedule (baking weekly):
- Keep in the fridge
- Take out 24 hours before baking
- Feed, wait for peak, then bake
- Feed again and return to fridge Vacation mode (2+ weeks away):
- Feed well, then refrigerate
- It can survive 2-4 weeks unfed in the fridge
- When you return: discard most, feed 2x daily for 2-3 days Drying for long-term storage:
- Spread thin on parchment paper
- Let dry completely (24-48 hours)
- Break into flakes, store in airtight container
- Can be revived months or even years later!
translation.lessonShort8: Solutions for the most common starter problems
translation.lessonContent8:
Don't panic! Most problems have simple solutions. Starter won't rise:
- Try a warmer spot (25-28°C)
- Switch to rye flour for a few feeds
- Use warmer water (28-30°C)
- Be patient — some starters take 10-14 days Brown liquid on top (hooch):
- Your starter is hungry! Stir it in or pour it off
- Feed more frequently or with more flour Strong acetone/nail polish smell:
- Very hungry! Feed immediately
- Feed twice daily for a few days Bubbles but no rise:
- The flour might be too weak (low protein)
- Try bread flour (12%+ protein) Mold (colored spots — green, black, pink):
- Unfortunately, throw it all away
- Start fresh — it's not your fault
- Mold is rare and usually from contamination Remember: consistency is more important than perfection. Keep feeding regularly and your starter will thrive.
translation.lessonShort9: How water source and feeding schedule affect results
translation.lessonContent9:
Water quality can make or break your starter. Chlorine & chloramine:
- City tap water often contains these disinfectants
- They can slow down or harm your starter culture
- Chlorine: let water sit uncovered for 24h — it evaporates naturally
- Chloramine (used by many modern water systems): does NOT evaporate — use a carbon filter or bottled water instead Water temperature for feeding:
- 25-30°C: Standard, promotes good activity
- 30-35°C: Speeds things up (useful in cold kitchens)
- Below 20°C: Significantly slows fermentation Feeding schedule tips:
- Feed at the same time every day for consistency
- A predictable schedule = a predictable starter
- If you miss a feeding, don't double up — just resume normally
- Watch your starter, not the clock. If it peaks faster, feed sooner The best water for your starter is whatever clean water is most accessible to you. Don't overthink it!
translation.lessonShort10: How different flours behave and when to use each
translation.lessonContent10:
Not all flour is created equal. White bread flour (11-13% protein):
- Best for daily feeding
- Predictable and consistent
- Produces a mild-flavored starter Whole wheat flour:
- More nutrients = faster fermentation
- Adds nuttiness and complexity
- Good for 10-20% of your feed mix Rye flour:
- The most nutrient-rich option
- Excellent for starting a new culture
- Creates a tangy, robust starter
- Great as 10-30% of your feed mix All-purpose flour (9-11% protein):
- Works fine but less structure than bread flour
- May rise less dramatically Protein content matters:
- Higher protein = more gluten = better structure
- Look for 11%+ protein on the label
- Strong bread flour gives the best results Experiment! Many bakers use a mix of flours for the best of all worlds.
translation.lessonShort11: How to control sourness and develop complex flavors
translation.lessonContent11:
Flavor is what makes sourdough special. You can control it! Two types of sourness:
- Lactic acid: Mild, creamy, yogurt-like (warm fermentation)
- Acetic acid: Sharp, tangy, vinegar-like (cool fermentation) For milder bread:
- Use warm water and a warm spot
- Feed more frequently
- Use white flour primarily
- Shorter bulk fermentation For tangier bread:
- Use cooler temperatures
- Longer fermentation times
- Add some rye or whole wheat flour
- Use a stiffer (lower hydration) starter Other flavor factors:
- Salt enhances and balances flavor (don't skip it!)
- Longer cold proofing in fridge = more complex flavors
- Different flours bring different flavor notes
- Longer autolyse = sweeter, more wheaty flavor Every bake is an experiment. Keep notes and dial in your perfect flavor!
translation.lessonContent12:
Good shaping creates structure and a beautiful loaf. Pre-shaping:
- Gently turn dough onto a floured surface
- Use a bench scraper to pull it into a rough ball
- Let it rest 15-20 min (bench rest) Final shaping (round loaf):
- Flip dough smooth-side down
- Fold sides to center, then roll into a ball
- Create surface tension by dragging toward you
- Place seam-side up in a floured banneton Scoring:
- Use a very sharp blade (razor blade or lame)
- Score just before putting in the oven
- Cut 1-2 cm deep at a 45-degree angle
- Classic: one curved slash across the top
- The score controls where the bread opens during baking Common mistakes:
- Too much flour on the surface = poor seal
- Over-handling = lost gas = dense bread
- Scoring too shallow = bread tears randomly Practice makes perfect. Your shaping will improve with every loaf!
translation.lessonShort13: How to fit sourdough into your weekly routine
translation.lessonContent13:
Sourdough fits any schedule with the right planning. Weekend baker (bake Saturday morning):
- Thursday evening: Take starter out of fridge, feed
- Friday morning: Feed starter (should be active)
- Friday afternoon: Mix dough when starter is at peak
- Friday evening: Stretch & fold, then overnight bulk
- Saturday morning: Shape, cold proof 1-2h, bake! Same-day bake:
- 7:00 AM: Feed starter
- 12:00 PM: Mix dough (starter at peak)
- 12:30 PM: Add salt after autolyse
- 1:00-3:00 PM: Stretch & fold sets
- 3:00 PM - overnight: Bulk fermentation
- Next morning: Shape and bake Tips for busy schedules:
- The fridge is your pause button
- Cold-proof shaped dough overnight for morning baking
- A well-fed starter can wait 1-2 hours past peak
- Make dough Friday night, bake fresh Saturday morning
translation.lessonShort14: Advanced techniques and next steps for your journey
translation.lessonContent14:
You've mastered the fundamentals! Here's where to go next. Level up your bread:
- Experiment with higher hydration (75-80%) for more open crumb
- Try overnight cold proofing for better flavor
- Add seeds, nuts, or dried fruit to your dough
- Experiment with different flour blends Expand your repertoire:
- Focaccia: Great beginner-friendly flatbread
- Pizza dough: Slow-fermented for incredible flavor
- Pancakes & waffles: Perfect use for discard
- Crackers: Simple and addictive
- Brioche: Rich, buttery bread Share the love:
- Give a piece of your starter to friends
- Teach someone to maintain their own
- Join a sourdough community online Keep learning:
- Every loaf teaches you something
- Take notes on what works
- Don't be afraid to experiment
- Remember: even a "bad" sourdough tastes amazing! Welcome to the sourdough family!
translation.milestoneSeedDesc: Your starter's first signs of life — tiny bubbles and initial fermentation!
translation.milestoneSeedTask: Mix 50g rye flour + 50g warm water (28°C). Cover loosely. Next day: discard half, add 50g flour + 50g water.
translation.milestoneSeedTip: Use rye flour for the first mix — it's packed with wild yeast. Use filtered or bottled water — chlorine can slow your starter. Keep it warm (24-26°C)!
translation.milestoneExpansionDesc: Your starter rises noticeably — 25-75% — after each feeding. Don't panic if it rose a lot early on (days 2-3) then went flat — this 'false rise' is normal!
translation.milestoneExpansionTask: Discard half, add 50g flour + 50g water. Mark the level with a rubber band. Does it rise 25-75% within 4-8 hours?
translation.milestoneExpansionTip: Consistent small bubbles mean the good bacteria are winning. Switch to white flour for predictability.
translation.milestoneStrengthDesc: Your starter reliably doubles in size — with visible bubbles and a pleasant tangy aroma!
translation.milestoneStrengthTask: Same feeding: discard half, 50g flour + 50g water. Does it double in 4-6 hours? Look for a domed top and lots of bubbles.
translation.milestoneStrengthTip: If it's not quite doubling yet, try warmer water (28-30°C) or a warmer spot. Consistency is key!
translation.milestoneBakeReadyDesc: Congratulations! Your starter doubles predictably, has a honeycomb texture, and smells pleasantly tangy. Time to bake!
translation.milestoneBakeReadyTask: Your starter is ready for bread! Check out the recipes section for your first bake.
translation.milestoneBakeReadyTip: Use your starter at peak (4-6h after feeding). Mark the level and learn its timing!
translation.celebrateSeedDesc: Your starter showed its first signs of life — bubbles mean bacteria are moving in!
translation.celebrateExpansionDesc: Your starter is rising consistently — the good bacteria are thriving!
translation.celebrateStrengthDesc: Your starter is reliably doubling — it's becoming a strong, mature culture!
translation.celebrateBakeReadyDesc: Your starter has graduated! It doubles predictably with beautiful bubbles and a wonderful aroma. Your first bread awaits!
translation.observationHint: Optional — helps track your starter's health over time
translation.insightEarly: Keep feeding daily — your starter is just getting started!
translation.insightNoObservations: Log your observations to get personalized tips!
translation.insightThriving: Your starter is thriving! Beautiful activity and great aroma.
translation.insightGrowing: Looking good! Your starter is getting stronger with each feeding.
translation.insightStruggling: Your starter needs some extra care — check the tips below.
translation.insightEarlyStage: This is normal for the early days. The beneficial bacteria are still settling in.
translation.insightReadyToBake: Your starter is showing all the signs of readiness — time to bake!
translation.tipStartObserving: Start noting what you see after each feeding — it helps you learn your starter's rhythm.
translation.tipWarmSpot: Try a warmer spot (25-28°C). A turned-off oven with just the light on works great!
translation.tipWholeGrainBoost: Add a tablespoon of whole grain or rye flour — it gives your starter a nutrient boost.
translation.tipConsistentFeeding: Feed at the same time each day. Consistency helps the good bacteria thrive.
translation.tipUnpleasantAromaNormal: Strong or odd smells are normal in the first few days as bacteria compete. It will improve!
translation.tipOverFermented: Very sour? Your starter may be hungry. Try feeding it more frequently or use cooler water.
translation.tipKeepGoing: You're on the right track! Keep up the daily feeding routine.
translation.tipPatience: Patience is key. Every starter develops at its own pace — keep feeding daily.
translation.tipEarlyDaysNormal: The first few days can be unpredictable. That's completely normal!
